CBS News live updates, 19 Oct 2026 13:05 GMT

Updated on:  October 19, 2026 / 1:05 PM EDT
            / CBS News

A major Saudi investment conference has been postponed to next year, its chief executive officer said on Monday, as the kingdom comes under repeated attacks from Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis.

Maha Al Saud, the CEO of the annual Future Investment Initiative (FII) Institute, said the event, which was scheduled to take place in Riyadh from Oct. 26 to 29, would instead happen in 2027 in a statement posted on X. She said organizers wanted to ensure the gathering's tenth anniversary edition delivered the "full scale" and "extraordinary quality" participants expected.

"This decision comes from a deep commitment to our partners, members, speakers and delegates," her statement said, adding: "A decade of partnership and shared vision deserves nothing less than our absolute best."

New conference dates will be announced soon, while current registrations and partnerships will remain valid, according to the statement.

For nearly a decade, the conference has served as a showcase for Saudi Arabia's efforts to attract global investors, business leaders and heads of state. The postponement dealt a blow to the kingdom's ambitions to draw foreign capital, diversify its oil-reliant economy and push its reform agenda.

Three sources familiar with the matter had earlier told AFP the conference would be postponed.

Egypt's parliament on Monday postponed its debate on President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's request to authorize military support to Saudi Arabia, which has faced mounting attacks from Yemen's Houthis, Egyptian state media reported. The debate has been delayed until next week, according to the report.

"House Speaker Hisham Badawi has adjourned the second parliamentary session dedicated to discussing authorisation for taking necessary measures to support and assist the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, with discussions set to resume on October 26," Egypt's state-run Al-Akhbar newspaper reported.

The postponement concluded a second day of parliamentary sessions in which Egyptian lawmakers weighed Sisi's request to approve support for Saudi Arabia, if requested by the kingdom. An emergency session on Sunday also ended without a decision.

Two lawmakers told AFP on Sunday that most parliamentarians supported the proposal, and a decision wasn't reached during that first session in order to "give all lawmakers the opportunity to speak and express their views."

The Egyptian Social Democratic Party, an opposition party with nearly a dozen seats in parliament, said it had instructed its parliamentary bloc to abstain from voting.

Although it described its solidarity with Saudi Arabia as "firm," the party said any deployment of Egyptian forces abroad should be guided by "specific objectives, clear information" and "an accurate assessment of the potential risks to the lives of our soldiers."

Yemen's Saudi-backed government claimed Monday to have killed 558 Houthi fighters over the past 24 hours. In a post on X, Col. Majed Al-Nazili said Yemeni forces had carried out 1,164 operations against the Iran-backed rebels.

"The operations resulted in neutralizing (558) militia elements, including field commanders," he wrote.

A major Saudi investment conference is set to be postponed, three sources briefed on the matter told the French news agency AFP on Monday, amid repeated attacks on the kingdom by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

One source said the event "won't happen on time" and that organizers "won't announce a new date soon." A second source, who confirmed the event would be postponed, told AFP: "Who would be willing to risk flying to Riyadh these days?"

Saudi Arabia's Future Investment Initiative (FII) Institute hosts an annual forum often referred to as "Davos in the desert." The event typically draws foreign leaders and business titans, and this year it is  scheduled to be held in Riyadh from Oct. 26 to 29.

The Wall Street Journal reported that the conference would either be held online or postponed.

Iran's top diplomat on Monday accused the United States of being responsible for the insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz that has left the nearly-eight month conflict sparked by joint U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran unresolved, despite the cessation of major military operations.

"The war imposed by the United States and the Zionist regime [Israel], combined with the economic blockade [on Iran's ports], constitutes the principal source of insecurity in our region," said Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, echoing many similar statements by himself and other senior Iranian figures.

He made the remark Monday during a joint news conference with his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov, who arrived in Tehran earlier Monday for his first visit since the outbreak of the war, as Russia tries to frame itself as a potential mediator despite close ties with the Iranian regime.

Lavrov was also scheduled to meet Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian during his visit, according to Russia's foreign ministry. The veteran Russian diplomat said Moscow's efforts were "aimed at preventing the return of a large-scale war," with talks between Tehran and Washington at a standstill.

Iran's Acting Oil Minister Hamid Bovard met Qatar's Minister of State for Energy Affairs, Saad Sherida al-Kaabi, in Doha on Monday to discuss energy relations and cooperation between the two countries.

According to Iran's official news agency IRNA, al-Kaabi confirmed the meeting, which focused on bilateral energy ties and opportunities for cooperation.

The death toll from a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's government-controlled Shabwa province rose to 50 on Monday, a government official told the French news agency AFP, after military sources earlier put the toll at more than 30.

The Iran-backed rebels fired ballistic missiles at the al-Alam military camp in the southern province of Shabwa.

"The death toll has risen to at least 50, with more than 100 people injured, some of them in critical condition," said Fahad al-Khalifi, deputy governor of Shabwa.

He added that hospitals in the province were overwhelmed and had been forced to transfer the most seriously wounded to facilities in neighbouring Hadramout and Aden.

Iran-backed Houthi rebels struck a military camp for government forces in southern Yemen on Monday, killing at least 20 soldiers, two Yemeni military officials said.

The rebels fired ballistic missiles at the al-Alam military camp in the southern province of Shabwa in an attack that left at least two dozen more troops wounded, the officials said.

The military officials with the internationally recognized government of Yemen spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to brief the media.

Yemen's decade-long civil war has intensified and become intertwined with the wider regional conflict sparked by the U.S. war with Iran over the last few months, as the Houthis, considered one of Iran's most potent proxy forces, attacks the government's Saudi backers on their home turf.

Houthi strikes on Saudi infrastructure, including civilian airports, have killed more than 20 people in recent weeks, and President Trump has said he's considering joining Saudi operations against the rebels. The Houthis have warned that if the U.S. does intervene, it would prompt a  "swift and painful" retaliation against U.S. personnel and interests across the region.

Oil prices were down early Monday, with Brent crude, the international standard, falling 2.5% to $107.16 per barrel and benchmark U.S. crude dropping 2.2% to $96.84 per barrel.

The prices fell after President Trump late Friday signed an executive order to put new U.S. sanctions against Russia on hold just days before they were to come into effect, drawing disappointment from Ukraine, with the move likely resulting in more energy exports from Russia.

Mr. Trump's decision came not long after he said earlier this month he had reached a diesel deal with Russia in an attempt to bring down elevated U.S. fuel prices ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

But despite Mr. Trump's controversial efforts to ease energy costs for Americans, oil prices have remained much higher compared to before the Iran war, due in large part to the ongoing risks to the supply chain caused by the crisis in the Middle East.

On Friday the price of Brent crude hit nearly $110 a barrel, its highest level since mid-May.

A tug boat traveling near the Strait of Hormuz was struck by two unknown projectiles, a British maritime monitoring agency said Sunday.

The U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center (UKMTO) said in a statement that a tugboat traveling southbound off the coast of the United Arab Emirates "reported being struck by two unknown projectiles."

"The tug has sustained damage but is continuing on its route," the agency said, "one minor casualty has been reported."

Last week saw 10 attacks on commercial vessels in and near the strait, according to the UKMTO, which said October has already become the worst month for attacks on shipping in the strait since the early days of the war in March.

The U.S. issued a security alert on Monday urging Americans in the Middle East to "exercise heightened vigilance."

"Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," the statement said.
